Tutorial 4: Variable Creation and Temporal Aggregation

climasus4r Team

13/09/2026

Source: vignettes/04-variaveis-agregacao.Rmd
04-variaveis-agregacao.Rmd

Objective

By the end of this tutorial you will be able to transform individual microdata into a time series ready for analysis. There are two chained operations and two visualization steps:

  1. Create derived variables — sus_data_create_variables() — generating age groups (user-defined, climate risk-based, and IBGE five-year bands) and calendar variables (year, month, quarter, season);
  2. Aggregate over time and space — sus_data_aggregate() — converting the individual records into counts per period and per municipality (daily, monthly, seasonal, etc.);
  3. Visualize the time series — sus_data_plot_aggregate_ts() — with epidemic curves, seasonal boxplots, calendar heatmaps and annual trends;
  4. Visualize the spatial distribution — sus_data_plot_aggregate_map() — with bubble maps or municipal choropleths.

This is the fourth stage of the pipeline (derive → aggregate). It occupies a critical place: this is where the data stop being a table of individual events and take on the shape required by the climate–health models of Tutorial 9 (a count YtY_t per time unit tt).

Scientific context

Time series studies in environmental epidemiology model the outcome count per period (e.g., deaths per day) as a function of environmental exposure (temperature, pollution). To do so, microdata must be aggregated onto a regular temporal grid and, often, stratified by age group, since vulnerability to heat and cold varies greatly with age (Gasparrini et al., 2015; Bhaskaran et al., 2013).

Two methodological decisions at this stage have direct consequences for the analysis:

  • The temporal aggregation unit (time_unit) defines the study’s resolution. Daily series capture short-term acute effects (ideal for DLNM); monthly or seasonal series highlight long-term patterns and seasonality (Bhaskaran et al., 2013).
  • Filling in missing dates (complete_dates = TRUE) guarantees a series without gaps: days with no deaths receive a zero count. Without this, time series models would mistakenly interpret the absence of a date as an absence of information, rather than as a genuine zero.

Age groups follow recognized categorizations — including the IBGE five-year structure (0–4, 5–9, …, 80+), which ensures national and international comparability — and a climate risk band (0–4, 5–64, 65+) designed to highlight the most vulnerable groups (IBGE, 2010; WHO, 2014).

Guiding case. We investigate temperature and health outcomes in the elderly (60+) in the São Paulo Metropolitan Region, 2014–2019. Starting from the elderly respiratory deaths already filtered in Tutorial 3 (caso_filtrado.rds), we create age groups (60–69, 70–79, 80+) and calendar variables, and aggregate into a daily series (all deaths) and a monthly series by age group. The resulting series (caso_serie.rds) feeds into the spatial join (Tutorial 5) and, later, the modeling (Tutorial 9).

Data used

Item Detail
Input dados/caso_filtrado.rds (output of Tutorial 3)
Outcome Respiratory deaths (ICD-10 J00–J99) in elderly 60+
System SIM-DO (mortality)
Scope São Paulo Metropolitan Region, 2014–2019
Output dados/caso_serie.rds (input for Tutorial 5)

If Tutorial 3 has not yet been run, the generation script warns and proceeds with a minimal synthetic example that has the same standardized column structure (data_obito, codigo_municipio_residencia, idade, sexo, causa_basica) — so the stage is illustrated end to end.

Complete pipeline

The blocks below reproduce what the script scripts/tutorial_04_variaveis_agregacao.R runs. Start by loading the package:

library(climasus4r)

Load the output from the previous stage 

caso_filtrado <- sus_data_read("output/caso_filtrado.parquet")
# or, in the tutorial workflow, readRDS("vignettes-pt/dados/caso_filtrado.rds")
obitos <- caso_filtrado            # climasus_df at stage "filter_cid"/"stand"

Create derived variables

sus_data_create_variables() creates age groups and calendar variables in a single call. Here we use bands geared to the elderly age range of the guiding case and link the seasonal variables to the "sudeste" (Southeast) climate region.

obitos_vars <- sus_data_create_variables(
  obitos,
  create_age_groups    = TRUE,
  age_breaks           = c(60, 70, 80, Inf),     # young-old / 70-79 / 80+
  age_labels           = c("60-69", "70-79", "80+"),
  create_calendar_vars = TRUE,                   # year, month, quarter, ...
  create_climate_vars  = TRUE,                   # season of the year
  climate_region       = "sudeste",              # climate region of the case
  hemisphere           = "south",                # Brazil
  backend              = "tibble",
  lang                 = "pt"
)

In addition to age_group (defined by age_breaks/age_labels), the function automatically creates the climate risk band (grupo_risco_climatico) and the IBGE five-year band (faixa_etaria_ibge), and — with create_calendar_vars = TRUE — the variables ano, mes, trimestre (year, month, quarter) and the season of the year (estacao_climatica + estacao_seca_chuvosa when climate_region is provided; otherwise, estacao_astronomica).

Aggregate into a daily time series

sus_data_aggregate() converts the individual records into counts. With fun = "count" and the SIM system, the aggregated column is automatically named n_obitos. complete_dates = TRUE fills days with no deaths with zero.

serie_diaria <- sus_data_aggregate(
  obitos_vars,
  time_unit      = "day",      # one observation per day
  fun            = "count",    # count of deaths
  group_by       = NULL,       # aggregates on the detected municipality code
  complete_dates = TRUE,       # fills days with no event with zero
  backend        = "tibble",
  lang           = "pt"
)

Aggregate into a monthly series by age group

The same function, now stratified by age_group. This is the series saved for the next tutorial.

serie_mensal <- sus_data_aggregate(
  obitos_vars,
  time_unit      = "month",
  fun            = "count",
  group_by       = "age_group",   # age group created above
  complete_dates = TRUE,
  backend        = "tibble",
  lang           = "pt"
)

Visualize the time series

sus_data_plot_aggregate_ts() takes a climasus_df at the "aggregate" stage and produces publication-quality plots. plot_type accepts "epidemic", "seasonal", "heatmap" and "trend" (and combinations, via patchwork).

# Daily epidemic curve with loess smoothing
sus_data_plot_aggregate_ts(
  serie_diaria,
  plot_type     = "epidemic",
  smooth_method = "loess",
  palette       = "lancet",
  lang          = "pt"
)

# Boxplot of the monthly seasonal distribution
sus_data_plot_aggregate_ts(
  serie_diaria,
  plot_type = "seasonal",
  lang      = "pt"
)

Visualize the spatial distribution

sus_data_plot_aggregate_map() maps the counts by municipality. To do so, we aggregate while preserving the municipality code as the grouping variable.

serie_muni <- sus_data_aggregate(
  obitos_vars,
  time_unit = "month",
  fun       = "count",
  group_by  = "codigo_municipio_residencia",
  backend   = "tibble",
  lang      = "pt"
)

sus_data_plot_aggregate_map(
  serie_muni,
  map_type  = "bubble",     # does not require geobr/sf
  log_scale = TRUE,
  palette   = "YlOrRd",
  lang      = "pt"
)

At the end of this stage we have serie_mensal (by age group) and serie_muni (by municipality) — the temporal/spatial base that feeds the next tutorials.

Function features

sus_data_create_variables()

Creates derived variables from age and event date. Requires the data to be at the "stand" stage (or later).

Argument Essential? Description
df yes Standardized climasus_df (stage "stand"+)
create_age_groups yes Creates age_group, grupo_risco_climatico and faixa_etaria_ibge (default TRUE)
age_breaks optional Age group cut points; default c(0, 5, 15, 60, Inf)
age_labels optional Group labels; if NULL, generated from age_breaks
create_calendar_vars yes Creates ano, mes, trimestre, etc. (default TRUE)
create_climate_vars optional Creates the season of the year; requires create_calendar_vars = TRUE
climate_region optional Climate region ("norte", "nordeste", "centro-oeste", "sudeste", "sul"); defines dry/wet season
hemisphere optional "south" (default, Brazil) or "north"
age_col / date_col optional Force the age/date column; if NULL, auto-detects
backend optional "arrow" (lazy, default) or "tibble"
lang / verbose optional Language ("pt"/"en"/"es") and messages

Return: the climasus_df with the new columns and stage advanced to "derive". Age is determined by a hierarchy: (1) existing age column, (2) calculation from birth date and event date (gold standard), (3) decoding of the DATASUS age code (fallback).

sus_data_aggregate()

Aggregates individual microdata into a time series of counts. Requires stage "stand" (or later).

Argument Essential? Description
df yes climasus_df (output of standardization/filtering/derivation)
time_unit yes "day", "week", "month", "quarter", "year", "season", or multiples such as "5 days", "14 days", "3 months" (default "day")
fun optional "count" (default), "sum", "mean", "median", "min", "max", "sd", "q25", "q75", "q95", "q99", or a named list
group_by optional Stratification columns (e.g., c("age_group", "sexo")); NULL aggregates on the detected municipality
value_col only if fun != "count" Numeric column to aggregate
complete_dates recommended TRUE fills periods with no event with zero (default FALSE)
date_col optional Date column; if NULL, auto-detects by system
backend optional "arrow" (lazy, default) or "tibble"
lang / verbose optional Language and messages

Return: a climasus_df at the "aggregate" stage with a date column (start of the period), the group_by columns, and the count column named intelligently by system: n_obitos (SIM), n_internacoes (SIH), n_nascimentos (SINASC), n_casos (SINAN), n_procedimentos (SIA), n_estabelecimentos (CNES).

sus_data_plot_aggregate_ts()

Time series plots from a climasus_df at the "aggregate" stage.

Argument Description
df Aggregated climasus_df
value_col Outcome column; if NULL, auto-detects (n_obitos, n_casos, …)
plot_type "epidemic", "seasonal", "heatmap", "trend" (accepts several, via patchwork)
group_col / facet_col Column for color (epidemic/seasonal) and for panels (facet_wrap)
smooth_method / smooth_span Smoothing of the epidemic curve: "loess" (default), "gam", "lm", "none"
log_transform Applies log1p to the y-axis / fill
palette "lancet" (default), "nejm", "jco", "uchicago", "viridis"
city Filters municipalities (name or IBGE code) before plotting
interactive TRUE returns a plotly widget
lang / verbose Language and messages

Return: the ggplot2 object (or plotly if interactive = TRUE), invisibly; it also prints the plot. Does not change the stage of df.

sus_data_plot_aggregate_map()

Municipal map of the aggregated counts.

Argument Description
df Aggregated climasus_df with a municipality code column
value_col Outcome column; if NULL, auto-detects
map_type "bubble" (default, without geobr/sf), "choropleth", "quantile_choropleth"
rate_per_100k TRUE calculates incidence per 100,000 inhabitants (uses pop_25)
period Date or c(start, end) to filter before aggregating
city / top_n Restricts to municipalities; labels the top_n largest
state_borders Overlays state borders (via geobr)
palette RColorBrewer palette ("YlOrRd", "Blues", …) or "lancet"/"nejm"
log_scale log1p on the color scale (default TRUE)
interactive TRUE returns plotly
use_cache / cache_dir Cache of municipal metadata
lang / verbose Language and messages

Return: a ggplot2 object (or plotly). The choropleth requires the Suggests packages geobr and sf; if absent, the function falls back to the bubble map with a warning. It does not modify df nor advance the stage.

Formulas

The aggregated count of an outcome in period tt (with fun = "count") is simply the number of records whose date falls in that period:

Yt=∑i=1N𝟏[⌊di⌋u=t] Y_t \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{1}\!\left[\,\lfloor d_i \rfloor_{u} = t\,\right]

where did_i is the date of event ii, ⌊⋅⌋u\lfloor \cdot \rfloor_{u} rounds down to the start of the period at unit uu (time_unit), and 𝟏[⋅]\mathbf{1}[\cdot] is the indicator function.

The annual trend figure (plot_type = "trend") reports the year-over-year (YoY) percent change:

Δ%a=(YaYa−1−1)×100 \Delta\%_{a} \;=\; \left( \frac{Y_{a}}{Y_{a-1}} - 1 \right) \times 100

When rate_per_100k = TRUE in the map, the municipal incidence rate is

taxam=casosmpopm×105 \text{taxa}_{m} \;=\; \frac{\text{casos}_{m}}{\text{pop}_{m}} \times 10^{5}

Illustrated results

Figure 1. Daily epidemic curve of respiratory deaths in the elderly (60+) in the São Paulo Metropolitan Region, 2014–2019, generated by sus_data_plot_aggregate_ts(plot_type = "epidemic"). The area and the line show the daily count; the smoothed (loess) curve highlights the underlying trend.

Figure 2. Monthly seasonal distribution (sus_data_plot_aggregate_ts(plot_type = "seasonal")). The boxplots by month show the winter seasonality (June–August) of elderly respiratory mortality — the starting point of the climate–health hypothesis of the guiding case.

Figure 3. Monthly series stratified by the age groups created in sus_data_create_variables() (60–69, 70–79, 80+). It is this stratified structure that is saved to caso_serie.rds for the following tutorials.

Figure 4. Spatial distribution of deaths by municipality (sus_data_plot_aggregate_map(map_type = "bubble")). The size and color of the bubbles encode the total number of events per municipality in the São Paulo Metropolitan Region (log1p scale).

References

  • Bhaskaran, K., Gasparrini, A., Hajat, S., Smeeth, L., & Armstrong, B. (2013). Time series regression studies in environmental epidemiology. International Journal of Epidemiology, 42(4), 1187–1195.
  • Gasparrini, A., Guo, Y., Hashizume, M., Lavigne, E., Zanobetti, A., Schwartz, J., et al. (2015). Mortality risk attributable to high and low ambient temperature: a multicountry observational study. The Lancet, 386(9991), 369–375.
  • Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística (IBGE). (2010). Censo Demográfico 2010. Rio de Janeiro: IBGE.
  • World Health Organization (WHO). (2014). Quantitative risk assessment of the effects of climate change on selected causes of death, 2030s and 2050s. Geneva: WHO.
